Chapter 2: Transformers & LLMs

Attention, transformer blocks, encoder models, and multimodal inputs

← Text processing · Course home · Next: Training →

Why transformers replaced recurrent models

RNNs and LSTMs process one token after another. That makes training hard to parallelise and makes early context difficult to retain in long sequences. Transformers instead process a sequence in parallel and let every token selectively draw information from the tokens relevant to it. The trade-off is that full attention compares token pairs, so its cost grows roughly quadratically with sequence length.

1. Self-attention: query, key, and value

Each token embedding \(x\) is projected into three learned vectors:

  • Query \(q=xW_Q\): what the current token is looking for.
  • Key \(k=xW_K\): what another token offers for matching.
  • Value \(v=xW_V\): the content that can be gathered.

For each query, the model scores visible keys, normalises the scores with softmax, and uses the resulting weights to form a weighted sum of values:

\[\operatorname{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\operatorname{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V\]

Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) prevents large dot products from making softmax too extreme. In a decoder, a causal mask hides future tokens, so generation stays left-to-right. The resulting representation of a token is contextual: the word it can attend most strongly to the noun it refers to.

Multi-head attention repeats this process with several independent Q/K/V projections. Each head can focus on a different relationship, then the outputs are concatenated and projected back together.

2. The transformer block

An LLM begins with token IDs, looks up embeddings, and adds positional information. It then stacks many blocks:

token + position → multi-head attention → residual + normalisation
                 → feed-forward network → residual + normalisation

The feed-forward network (FFN) is a two-layer MLP applied independently to every token after attention has mixed contextual information. It provides nonlinearity and typically holds many of the model parameters.

Residual connections add a sublayer’s input to its output. They preserve useful signal and give gradients a shorter route through a deep network. LayerNorm stabilises each token’s activations across features; modern models often use the cheaper RMSNorm variant.

Attention itself has no sense of word order. Positional encodings solve that: the original transformer used sinusoidal vectors, BERT used learned positions, and many modern decoder models use RoPE, which rotates queries and keys according to position and handles relative distance well.

3. Encoder versus decoder

The original transformer had both components, but they are trained for different tasks.

Model type Visibility Objective Typical use
Encoder (BERT) Both left and right context Predict masked tokens Classification and embeddings
Decoder (GPT/Llama-style) Earlier tokens only Predict the next token Autoregressive generation

A decoder’s final linear layer produces one logit for every vocabulary token. Softmax turns logits into next-token probabilities; choosing a token and appending it repeats the generation loop. Decoding controls such as temperature, top-k, and top-p affect this selection at inference time.

4. Scaling attention efficiently

Full attention becomes expensive on long inputs. Important architectural responses include:

  • Sliding-window attention: each token attends to a local window, reducing the main cost toward linear growth; occasional global layers can retain wider links.
  • RoPE scaling: extends a model’s usable context beyond the length seen in training, with potential quality loss at extremes.
  • Mixture-of-Experts (MoE): routes each token to only a few specialised FFNs, raising total capacity while keeping computation per token relatively restrained.

5. BERT and contextual embeddings

BERT is a bidirectional encoder trained with masked-language modelling. It sees both sides of a missing word, which makes it suited to understanding an input rather than producing long text. Its input combines token, position, and segment embeddings, with special [CLS] and [SEP] tokens.

For classification, the [CLS] representation is commonly passed to a task head. For semantic representation, token vectors can also be mean-pooled. Reading the raw embedding layer gives a static vector; running the sequence through BERT’s transformer layers yields contextual vectors whose meaning changes with surrounding text.

6. Multimodal models

Modern systems can accept text and images together. An image encoder turns visual input into embeddings; a decoder then consumes the combined image-and-text representation to generate a response. This reuses the encoder and decoder ideas in a single multimodal flow.

Practice focus

The chapter lab uses BERT to inspect tokenisation, compare static and contextual embeddings with cosine similarity, and contrast [CLS] pooling with mean pooling. Be able to explain both the attention equation and the data flow through a full transformer block.
